questions.q: What is the key distinction between a credit memo and a debit memo in Payables?
options: A credit memo increases the balance owed; a debit memo decreases it
They are identical documents with two different names
A credit memo is issued by the supplier; a debit memo is issued by your own organization
A debit memo can only be used for tax corrections
questions.explain: Both reduce the amount owed; the distinction is who originates the document -- the supplier for a credit memo, your organization for a debit memo.

questions.q: How are credit memos and debit memos represented in Payables?
questions.explain: Both are entered as negative-amount invoices, which is how they reduce rather than add to the supplier balance.

questions.q: In the Solace Robotics example, a $15,000 invoice is followed by a $1,500 credit memo for defective units. What is the net amount owed?
questions.explain: $15,000 minus the $1,500 credit memo leaves $13,500 owed.

questions.q: Why might an organization issue its own debit memo instead of waiting for the supplier's credit memo?
options: Debit memos are required before any credit memo can be issued
To record the dispute and reduction on their own books even before the supplier agrees
Because debit memos are the only way to cancel an invoice
Because suppliers are not permitted to issue credit memos
questions.explain: A debit memo lets the organization's AP team record its position internally while collections or disputes with the supplier continue.

questions.q: Why is it useful to match a credit or debit memo back to the original invoice or PO?
options: It is purely cosmetic and has no practical benefit
It automatically changes the supplier's payment terms
It keeps the reduction tied to a specific transaction instead of an unexplained negative balance
It prevents the supplier from ever invoicing again
questions.explain: Matching the memo to its source transaction supports audit and account reconciliation later.
